criteria.criterion: Unit tests for the new helper pass under `cargo test`: over-limit text is cut at the last whitespace within 72 chars so no word is split; text at or under the limit is unchanged; a single over-long word is hard-cut at 72 chars; multibyte text does not panic.
criteria.evidence: Four tests in lib.rs truncate_tests (text_within_the_limit_is_unchanged, over_limit_text_is_cut_at_the_last_whitespace, a_single_over_long_word_is_hard_cut, multibyte_text_does_not_panic) ran and passed. They cover the at-limit case, a cut that lands exactly on a space, a leading-space over-long word, and both Latin-accent and CJK multibyte text. I also read the helper: it finds the char boundary with char_indices().nth(max), so slicing is always on a char boundary.
commands: cargo test --locked -p athena-core -- truncate_tests subject_tests a_long_reading_title

criteria.criterion: A `cargo test` test builds a long intervention subject (manage.rs) and a long reading title (reading.rs) from multi-word text and shows neither ends mid-word and both are at most 72 chars.
criteria.evidence: manage::subject_tests::a_long_intervention_subject_is_cut_at_a_word_boundary and reading::tests::a_long_reading_title_is_cut_at_a_word_boundary passed. Each checks that the output is at most 72 chars, is a prefix of the full text, and is followed by a space. By my hand count, the reading test would fail on the old take(72) code, which cut at 'middle o'. The manage test would not: see the minor finding.
commands: cargo test --locked -p athena-core -- truncate_tests subject_tests a_long_reading_title

criteria.criterion: The three `.chars().take(72)` sites (manage.rs subject, reading.rs title, store.rs title fallback) call the shared helper instead.
criteria.evidence: In the diff, manage.rs uses intervention_subject → crate::truncate_at_word, reading.rs uses reading_title → crate::truncate_at_word, and store.rs JobRecords::title calls crate::truncate_at_word directly. All three use crate::SUBJECT_MAX (72). A Grep for 'take\(72\)' across the tree finds no remaining code site.

criteria.criterion: `cargo clippy`, `cargo fmt --check` and the full `cargo test` all pass.
criteria.evidence: fmt printed nothing (exit 0). Clippy finished with no warnings. The full test suite reported 0 failed in every test binary; the only skips are tests already marked ignored. The non-quiet run's output was saved to a file outside the working directory that policy would not let me read, so I reran in quiet mode to see the results.

criteria.criterion: CHANGELOG.md notes that generated commit subjects and titles are cut at word boundaries.
criteria.evidence: Under ### Changed, CHANGELOG.md now says: 'Generated commit subjects and job titles are cut at word boundaries, not mid-word…'. It names the shared helper, says the limit is still 72, says a single over-long word is hard-cut, and cites n4. All of this matches the code.

findings.summary: The manage.rs subject test would also pass on the old take(72) code, so it does not prove the intervention-subject fix.
findings.evidence: By hand count, 'Record an intervention: ' is 24 chars, and in the test text 'never' ends at char 72 with a space after it. The old take(72) therefore produced '...it never', which already passes every assertion. The call site is plainly correct when read, and the helper and reading tests do catch a regression, but this input should be lengthened by a character or two so the naive cut lands mid-word.

summary: The change does what n4 asks. All three places that cut generated subjects and titles at 72 characters now call one shared helper, `truncate_at_word` in athena-core/src/lib.rs. That helper cuts at the last whitespace within the limit, cuts a single over-long word at exactly 72 characters, and handles multibyte text safely. The helper has unit tests, there is a test for the reading title, and CHANGELOG.md describes the change accurately. Only the five listed files changed. fmt, clippy and the full cargo test all pass when I ran them here. One minor weakness: the manage.rs subject test uses text whose old fixed-width cut already fell on a word boundary, so that test would not catch a return to the mid-word cut at that site. Verdict: pass.
